questions.question_text: Kharif vs Rabi cropping season timing.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Kharif: Sown June-July (monsoon), harvested Sept-Oct. Rabi: Sown Oct-Dec (winter), harvested April-June.
Traditional slash-and-burn shifting agriculture in North-Eastern states.
Hot & humid climate (>25°C), rainfall >100 cm, clayey alluvial soil with high water retention. Leading states: WB, UP, Punjab.
Cool growing season (10-15°C), bright sunshine at ripening (21-26°C), 50-75 cm rainfall. Leading states: Punjab, Haryana, UP.

questions.question_text: Technological and institutional reforms in Indian agriculture.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Institutional: Land consolidation (Chakbandi), abolition of Zamindari. 2. Credit: Kisan Credit Card (KCC), PAIS. 3. Market: Minimum Support Price (MSP). 4. Tech: HYV seeds, chemical fertilizers, drip irrigation. 5. Media: Weather bulletins via radio/TV.

questions.question_text: Impact of Green Revolution on Indian agriculture.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Positive: Achieved food self-sufficiency, boosted wheat/rice yields via HYV seeds & fertilizers.
Negative: Caused falling water tables, soil salinization, land degradation in Punjab/Haryana, and widened income disparity between large & small farmers.

question_papers.paper_title: Set 3 - Agriculture: Substance vs Commercial Systems

questions.question_text: Leading producer of Pulses in India?
Oilseed used both as Kharif and Rabi crop?

questions.marking_scheme_answer: Primitive: Small plots, manual tools, rain-fed, self-consumption. Commercial: Large plots, HYV seeds, fertilizers, machinery, market sale.

questions.question_text: Why pulses are grown in crop rotation.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Pulses are leguminous crops whose root nodules host Rhizobium bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen, restoring soil fertility.

Jowar, Bajra, and Ragi are coarse grains with high nutritional value. Jowar is 3rd most important food crop (rain-fed in Maharashtra). Bajra grows on sandy/black soils (Rajasthan). Ragi grows in dry red/black soils (Karnataka).

questions.question_text: Evaluate the challenges faced by Indian farmers today.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Declining public investment in agricultural infrastructure & irrigation. 2. High cost of inputs (HYV seeds, fertilizers, diesel). 3. Reduction in fertilizer subsidies increasing cost of production. 4. Severe competition from international agricultural imports. 5. Unpredictable weather & climate change risks.

questions.question_text: Which crop is both food and fodder?

questions.marking_scheme_answer: The rearing of silkworms on mulberry leaves for the commercial production of silk fiber.

questions.question_text: State two objectives of Minimum Support Price (MSP).
questions.marking_scheme_answer: 1. Protect farmers from distress sales during harvest glut. 2. Guarantee floor price security for key crops.

questions.question_text: Impact of Globalization on Indian agriculture.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Exposed Indian farmers to international competition. Forced focus on high-value organic crops, bio-farming, and export commodities (spices, tea, fruits), but hurt smallholders unable to compete with subsidized Western farm imports.

questions.question_text: Detailed structural breakdown of major beverage crops: Tea and Coffee.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Tea: Tropical/subtropical plant requiring warm moist frost-free climate, deep well-drained loamy soil, high rainfall evenly distributed. Labor-intensive. Leading state: Assam.
Coffee: Indian Arabica variety imported from Yemen. Cultivated on hill slopes of Baba Budan Hills and Nilgiris in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu.

questions.case_passage:
Right of inheritance led to land division among heirs, creating tiny unviable plots requiring Chakbandi.
Q1. Cause of small farm size? (1m)
Q2. Solution implemented by government? (2m)
Q3. Why small farms hinder mechanization? (1m)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Right of inheritance dividing land among heirs.
2. Consolidation of holdings (Chakbandi).
3. Tiny scattered plots make using tractors, perimeter fencing, and efficient irrigation difficult.

questions.question_text: Compare Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid seasons.
questions.marking_scheme_answer: Kharif: Monsoon (June-Oct), Paddy/Cotton. Rabi: Winter (Oct-June), Wheat/Mustard. Zaid: Summer (March-June), Watermelon/Cucumber.

questions.question_text: Comprehensive analysis of Non-Food crops: Rubber, Cotton, Jute.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Rubber: Equatorial crop, humid climate, >200cm rain, >25°C temp. Used in auto tires. State: Kerala.
Cotton: Kharif crop, black soil, 210 frost-free days, bright sunshine. State: Maharashtra/Gujarat.
Jute: Golden fiber, high temp, fertile alluvial soil. Used in gunny bags, ropes, carpets. State: West Bengal.

questions.case_passage:
Organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals, using biological inputs and traditional seeds.
Q1. Define Organic Farming. (1m)
Q2. Two environmental benefits? (2m)
Q3. Economic advantage for farmers? (1m)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Farming without synthetic fertilizers or chemical pesticides using natural organic inputs.
2. Preserves soil micro-organisms and prevents chemical runoff into water bodies.
3. High demand for organic produce fetches premium export prices.
